321.quote_or_event: “You kill living beings, and call it a righteous action. Tell me, brother, what would you call an unrighteous action?”
321.explanation: Kabir confronts those who kill animals in sacrifice and call it dharma, turning the question back on them: if killing is righteousness, what is left to call sin?
321.tie_back: The Kural answers 'what is virtue?' with 'not killing'; Kabir reaches the same point from the other side, insisting that killing cannot be called righteousness.
321.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
321._accuracy_note: A strong fit; Kabir's target is ritual killing presented as religion, and Sikh teaching as a whole does not define virtue as non-killing in the Kural's absolute way.

322.quote_or_event: Every gurdwara keeps a langar, a free communal kitchen where food is served to all who come, seated together in a line so that no one claims higher or lower status. Britannica notes that under Guru Amar Das visitors ate in the casteless langar, and that the langar originated as a protest against the caste system.
322.explanation: The langar puts vand chhakna, sharing what one has, at the centre of Sikh worship: no one who comes is turned away hungry.
322.tie_back: The Kural ranks sharing one's food first among the virtues the learned have gathered; the Sikh langar makes that sharing a permanent institution open to all.
322.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'langar' (with linked coverage in 'Guru Amar Das' and 'Sikhism: The rejection of caste') (paraphrase)
322._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the Kural's first half, sharing food; it does not address the second half, protecting the many forms of life.

323.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
323.explanation: Guru Nanak places truth, and above all a life lived in truth, at the very top of the spiritual life.
323.tie_back: The Kural ranks non-killing first and truthfulness second; Guru Nanak's ranking differs, placing truthful living above everything, so the parallel lies in the shared high esteem for truth rather than in the order.
323.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
323._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikh teaching puts truthful living at the summit and has no verse ranking non-killing above truth, so this is a partial contrast more than a parallel.

324.quote_or_event: “And when, O Nanak, he is merciful to all beings, only then shall he be called a Muslim.”
324.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines what makes a person truly religious: not outward forms but mercy towards every living being.
324.tie_back: The Kural defines the good path as the way that takes care not to kill any creature; Guru Nanak likewise makes mercy to all beings the defining mark of the true religious path.
324.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
324._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: mercy to all beings implies avoiding harm, but the verse does not speak of killing specifically and is framed as a definition of a true Muslim.

325.quote_or_event: “You call yourself the most excellent sage; then who would you call a butcher?”
325.explanation: Kabir mocks those who kill in religious sacrifice yet claim the rank of the highest sages: by their deeds they are no different from butchers.
325.tie_back: The Kural ranks highest among renunciants the one who fears the sin of killing; Kabir denies the title of great sage to anyone who kills, whatever his religious standing.
325.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1103, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
325._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on holy status being cancelled by killing; note that Sikhism rejects the renunciant path the Kural presupposes, and Kabir's target is sacrificial killing.

326.quote_or_event: “The Messenger of Death does not approach those who are pleasing to the Lord God.”
326.explanation: Gurbani repeatedly promises that Death's messenger cannot come near those who live in God's favour; Sikh commentators usually read this as freedom from spiritual death and the fear of death.
326.tie_back: The Kural says devouring Death will not advance on the days of one who keeps to non-killing; Guru Arjan makes a similar promise of protection from Death for the one pleasing to God.
326.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 401, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
326._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the image of Death kept at bay matches, but the condition in Gurbani is God's favour through Naam, not non-killing, and the sense is spiritual rather than a longer life.

327.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
327.explanation: In his saloks Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the spiritually wise person as one who neither threatens others nor is cowed by threats. He himself chose execution in 1675 rather than yield, accepting death rather than inflicting it.
327.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking another's life even at the cost of one's own; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal of never terrorising others, and his own martyrdom, come close to that self-sacrificing non-violence.
327.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
327._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Sikh teaching does not forbid all killing absolutely; the later Gurus permitted armed defence as a last resort, so the Kural's rule is stricter than Sikh doctrine.

328.quote_or_event: Macauliffe tells of Shaikh Sajjan, a robber who built a temple and a mosque for travellers, then threw his guests into a well at night and kept their property. After hearing Guru Nanak's hymn he confessed his murders; the Guru had him bring out all the goods of his victims and give them to the poor, and he became the Guru's follower.
328.explanation: The story shows wealth gained through killing as wholly worthless: it cannot be kept, only given away in repentance.
328.tie_back: The Kural says that however great the gain, profit won by killing is the lowest of things to the noble; Guru Nanak made Sajjan give up every coin he had gained that way.
328.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 45-47 (paraphrase)
328._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on gain through killing being worthless; the story belongs to the Janamsakhi tradition and is hagiography rather than documented history.

329.quote_or_event: “Those who suck the blood of human beings-how can their consciousness be pure?”
329.explanation: Guru Nanak declares that those who live by preying on others cannot have a pure mind, whatever outward rituals they keep.
329.tie_back: The Kural calls those who make killing their work doers of base deeds in the eyes of the discerning; Guru Nanak likewise judges those who live off others' blood as inwardly impure.
329.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
329._accuracy_note: Next-best: 'sucking blood' is a metaphor for exploitation (Sikh commentators read it as bribery and oppression), not literally the trade of killing animals that the Kural condemns.

330.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, they oppress living beings and kill them, and call it proper. When the Lord calls for their account, what will their condition be?”
330.explanation: Kabir warns that those who kill living beings by force and justify it as lawful must still answer for it when their deeds are reckoned.
330.tie_back: The Kural says the wise see wretched, diseased lives as the fruit of having taken life from bodies; Kabir likewise warns that killing is entered in the account and its consequence will come.
330.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1375, Salok Bhagat Kabir, Salok 199 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
330._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both teach that killing brings a reckoning, but Kabir does not name disease or poverty in a later life as the specific consequence.
